stories.title: South Beach’s Cameo Theater Could Reopen With Romain Zago Concept
stories.excerpt: Nightlife operator Romain Zago wants to reopen the historic Cameo Theater in South Beach seven years after its nightclub shuttered. Zago, who made a name for himself owning the nearby Mynt Lounge nightclub, has filed plans to turn the Art Deco theater at 1445 Washington Avenue into a 466-seat restaurant and lounge. The plans call for a bar and lounge with 226 seats on the ground floor, with the existing stage remaining. The second floor will house a 240-seat restaurant. MainRo, a club and restaurant Zago launched in Hollywood, Calif., will likely serve as the template for the 17,589-square-foot venue, which has a license to sell alcohol until 5 A.M., according to a filing with the Miami Beach Planning Board, which will hear the proposal on Nov. 3. “The applicant proposes a refined dining-and-entertainment destination in the tradition of the grand European supper houses — a modern Moulin Rouge by way of Cirque du Soleil,” the application states. “The concept merges a full-service luxury restaurant with a reservation-driven entertainment lounge, anchored by live theatrical performance rather than open dance floor.” The application also suggests Miami real estate investor and developer Michael Konig is a partner in the venture. Cameo Theater has been a fixture in South Beach nightlife since it was built in 1938, although it has remained mostly vacant since 2019 when the Cameo nightclub closed. Zori Hayon has owned the property since at least the 1980s. Zago, who hails from France, owned and operated Mynt Lounge until selling the nightclub in 2024. He launched MainRo two years earlier. Attorney Bob de la Fuente of Lehtinen Schultz, who represents the applicant, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Romain Zago reopening Cameo Theater, South Beach Miami as 466-seat restaurant-lounge.
Historic venue conversion signals recovery and nightlife/dining tenant demand in South Beach.
Limited direct multifamily impact; hospitality/retail amenity play, not residential supply or demand driver.
stories.summary: Nightlife operator Romain Zago is repositioning the shuttered Cameo Theater in Miami's South Beach into a 466-seat restaurant and lounge modeled on European supper clubs. The 17,589-square-foot Art Deco space will feature a ground-floor bar (226 seats) and second-floor restaurant (240 seats), with extended alcohol license until 5 A.M. The Miami Beach Planning Board will hear the proposal on November 3.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. While hospitality/dining recovery signals economic confidence in South Beach, this is a single-asset retail conversion with no housing supply or demand implications for the Miami submarket.

stories.title: McKinney’s Cannon Beach Reaches Construction Milestone
stories.excerpt: In what can be called the inverse of topping out, construction crews have completed digging a big hole in McKinney for a surf lagoon. The Dallas Business Journal reports the $200 million project, dubbed Cannon Beach, will include the 3.3-acre surf pool, a lazy river, cliff-jump platforms, a sandy beach and cabanas, along with restaurants, shops, an indoor action sports facility, a spa, a resort hotel and office space. The surf pool will cost $6 million. Construction is expected to wrap up in March 2027. The overall development is expected to take about four years to complete. Once opened, Cannon Beach could attract about 400,000 visitors annually and generate more than $2 billion in economic impact over the next two decades. Cross Architects is leading the design. Cannon Beach is a partnership between Cannon, the city of McKinney, the McKinney EDC⁠ and the McKinney Community Development Corp. The post McKinney’s Cannon Beach Reaches Construction Milestone appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Cannon Beach, McKinney: $200M mixed-use with surf lagoon, resort, office; 400K annual visitors forecast.
Project completion March 2027; expect $2B economic impact over 20 years; 4-year construction timeline.
Major destination draw signals McKinney population/employment growth; indirect residential demand lift in Dallas metro.
stories.summary: Cannon Beach, a $200 million mixed-use development in McKinney, Texas, has completed site excavation for its 3.3-acre surf pool core asset. The project includes a lazy river, sandy beach, 40-acre green space, resort hotel, office, spa, and action sports facility. Construction wraps March 2027 and is projected to attract 400,000 annual visitors and generate $2 billion in economic impact over two decades.
stories.impact: Destination amenity development signals McKinney's growth trajectory and appeal to young, affluent households. The forecast 400K annual visitors and resort hotel anchor suggest population in-migration and office/employment expansion in the North Dallas suburb, creating a secondary demand spike for rental housing in McKinney and nearby submarkets ahead of the 2027 opening.

stories.title: OHT Helming 402-Unit Austin Rental Community
stories.excerpt: OHT Partners broke ground on The Barton, a 402-unit multifamily community on more than 60 acres in Southwest Austin. Located at 8956 W. State Highway 71, The Barton will feature a mix of three-story garden-style buildings and two-story townhomes with more than 40 acres designated as green space. Design features include large floor plans, private yards and tuck-under garages. The Barton will include one-, two- and three-bedroom residences ranging from 702 to 1,584 square feet. Thirty residences will be townhomes, while select units will feature private yards and tuck-under garages. Community amenities will include two resort-style pools, a 9,000-square-foot clubhouse, a 1,500-square-foot fitness center, 1,500 square feet of coworking space, two pickleball courts, a 1.4-acre dog park, an expansive trail system and multiple community courtyards. OHT anticipates delivering the first residences in the first quarter of 2028 and completing the community in the fourth quarter of 2028. The Barton project team includes Developer/General Contractor OHT Partners and Architect Meeks + Partners. The post OHT Helming 402-Unit Austin Rental Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: OHT Partners breaks ground: The Barton, 402 units, Southwest Austin (Hwy 71), 60+ acres.
Delivery Q1 2028; garden-style + townhomes, 40 acres green space, premium amenities (pools, fitness, coworking).
Confirms developer confidence in Southwest Austin rental demand; garden-style positioning targets lifestyle/family segment.
stories.summary: OHT Partners broke ground on The Barton, a 402-unit garden-style and townhome community on 60+ acres in Southwest Austin at State Highway 71. Units range from 702 to 1,584 square feet (one to three bedrooms); 30 are townhomes with private yards and tuck-under garages. Amenities include two pools, 9,000-square-foot clubhouse, coworking, dog park, and trail system. First deliveries Q1 2028; project completion Q4 2028.
stories.impact: Validates strong rental demand in Southwest Austin submarket and developer appetite for larger, lower-density garden-style product. The emphasis on floor plan size, private outdoor space, and coworking signals tenant preference for suburban flexibility—key indicator that Austin's outer rings remain absorption-ready heading into 2028.

stories.title: Italian Restaurant Casa Serra to Open at 227 Front Street in South Street Seaport
stories.excerpt: Lower Manhattan’s South Street Seaport will be living la dolce vita with its latest restaurant lease. Casa Serra, a sister restaurant to East Village eatery House of Pasta, has inked a 2,824-square-foot lease at the Durst Organization’s 227 Front Street, the landlord announced Tuesday. The 15-year lease has an asking rent of $100 per square foot. “Historic Front Street has seen strong momentum in retail leasing this year with the arrival of Kee’s Chocolates, Mesa Bar and now Casa Serra,” Jody Durst, president of the Durst Organization, said in a statement. “Lower Manhattan brings together a growing residential population, tourism and returning office tenants that all enjoy these new dining and retail concepts.” Casa Serra, or “greenhouse” in Italian, is expected to open this winter and will feature popular dishes from House of Pasta, including mushroom and truffle white lasagna, bucatini alla pistachio, and chicken milanese with fettuccine al burro. Durst was represented in-house by Karen Rose and by KSR’s Zach Nathan, Brandon Berger and Hunter Lazan. “We’ve seen a lot of momentum on Front Street,” Nathan told Commercial Observer. “There’s been strong interest from good operators who see what we see in the Seaport and believe in the direction of the neighborhood. Durst has been very thoughtful about the tenant mix and finding the right operators for these spaces. ” KSR’s Jack Hamadani, who represented the tenant in this deal, added that Casa Serra’s ownership “saw an opportunity to expand their concept into a neighborhood that continues to gain momentum.” Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Casa Serra (House of Pasta sister): 2,824 SF lease, 227 Front Street, South Street Seaport.
$100/SF asking rent; 15-year term; opening winter 2024; chef-driven Italian concept.
Signals retail recovery in Lower Manhattan driven by returning office tenants and growing residential base.
stories.summary: Casa Serra, a sister restaurant to House of Pasta, has leased 2,824 square feet at Durst Organization's 227 Front Street in South Street Seaport under a 15-year lease at $100 per square foot. The Italian restaurant opens this winter and joins recent arrivals Kee's Chocolates and Mesa Bar. Durst noted momentum from lower Manhattan's growing residential population, tourism, and returning office tenants.
stories.impact: Restaurant leasing momentum in South Street Seaport reflects recovery in Lower Manhattan's residential population and office occupancy—both dependent on multifamily supply in the submarket. Increasing retail demand and rents signal landlord confidence in sustained residential growth and worker return, justifying multifamily development and conversion plays in Lower Manhattan.

stories.title: AXS Fund Picks Up 20-Story Phoenix Office Asset
stories.excerpt: AXS Opportunity Fund acquired One North Central, a 429,120-square-foot, 20-story Class A office tower located at 1 North Central Avenue in the heart of Downtown Phoenix. Newmark’s Chris Marchildon, Barry Gabel and CJ Osbrink represented the seller, Parallel Capital Partners, who bought the building for $93 million in 2015. Constructed in 2001, the tower has access to the Valley Metro light rail system, nearby entertainment venues, government offices and educational institutions. The property also includes a recently completed amenity center, structured and subterranean parking, and ground-floor retail offerings. AXS Opportunity Fund has retained Newmark’s Brett Abramson, Chris Latvaaho and Chris Beall as the leasing advisors for the property. Marchildon added, “As capital continues to return to the office sector, properties with strong fundamentals and irreplaceable downtown locations are attracting increased attention from buyers.” The post AXS Fund Picks Up 20-Story Phoenix Office Asset appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: AXS Opportunity Fund acquires One North Central, 429K SF, 20-story Class A office, Downtown Phoenix.
Purchase price undisclosed; seller Parallel Capital paid $93M in 2015; building completed 2001.
Office capital returning to irreplaceable downtown locations; limited multifamily relevance unless conversion target.
stories.summary: AXS Opportunity Fund acquired One North Central, a 429,120-square-foot, 20-story Class A office tower at 1 North Central Avenue in Downtown Phoenix. The 2001-built property includes ground-floor retail, structured/subterranean parking, and recent amenity center upgrades. It sits near Valley Metro light rail, entertainment, and government offices. Parallel Capital sold after owning since 2015 (at $93 million).
stories.impact: Limited direct impact. While office capital returning to downtown locations signals growing Phoenix metro confidence, this is a pure-play office asset with no housing supply or demand signal. Downtown Phoenix may see ancillary demand from office workers if densification/mixed-use conversion occurs, but article provides no evidence of that.

stories.title: Financial District’s 70 Broad Street Purchased at Steep Discount
stories.excerpt: An undisclosed buyer has paid $9.35 million to purchase the landmarked American Bank Note Company Building at 70 Broad Street in Manhattan’s Financial District, Commercial Observer has learned. It’s a steep discount from both the $88 million the five-story property originally hit the market for in 2016 and the $20 million former lender Wilmington Trust paid for it in an auction last year. The buyer was represented by Louis Franco and Joseph Isa of Isa Realty Group along with attorney Eric S. Schoenfeld of Tannenbaum Helpern. The buyer plans to reposition the 19,478 square-foot 70 Broad Street, which sits between Beaver and Marketfield streets and was once home to a bank note maker. Their exact plans for the long-vacant property are unclear, but the first, second and lower levels have commercial spaces. A private elevator leads to three full-floor residential units on the third through fifth floors. The Neoclassical property was designed in the early 1900s by Kirby, Petit & Green to be the American Bank Note Company’s administrative and sales offices. It has two long, formidable columns, as commonly used by financial institutions, as well as a carved eagle over its doorway. The company produced currency, stock certificates and other materials that require engraved printing. The building sold to the Bank of Tokyo in 1988 and was later purchased by fast-food franchisers Murray and Irving Riese for $3.5 million. Tony Goldman, later the creator of Wynwood in Miami, bought the property in 1995 for $1.3 million for a restaurant and his offices. More recently, a Chinese investment group affiliated with the Chen family and Winta Asset Management acquired the property for approximately $18 million in 2010 and subsequently undertook a major renovation and repositioning. In 2015, Winta financed the property with a $15 million loan originated by Silverpeak Real Estate Finance, which was subsequently securitized. bullets: 70 Broad Street, Manhattan Financial District: $9.35M purchase; landmarked 19,478 SF, 5-story mixed-use.
Steep discount from $88M (2016) and $20M (2024 lender sale); buyer plans repositioning.
Distressed asset, long-vacant; residential component (3 full-floor units upper floors) unclear in reposition strategy.
stories.summary: An undisclosed buyer purchased 70 Broad Street, a landmarked American Bank Note Company Building in Manhattan's Financial District, for $9.35 million—a sharp drop from the $88 million asking price in 2016 and $20 million paid by lender Wilmington Trust at auction in 2024. The 5-story, 19,478-square-foot Neoclassical property contains ground-floor commercial space and three full-floor residential units on upper floors. The buyer's repositioning plans are unclear.
stories.impact: Significant distress signal in Manhattan Financial District multifamily. The steep markdown and extended vacancy suggest weak demand for small-scale, mixed-use residential assets in the submarket. Likely redevelopment/repositioning target, but uncertainty around buyer intent and historic landmark constraints limit predictability of multifamily supply impact; signals market softness rather than opportunity.

stories.title: LogiPropCo Adding 1.2M-SF Logistics Facility to Phoenix Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Logistics Property Company (LogiPropCo) closed on a 76-acre site at the intersection of Interstate 10 and Perryville Road in Buckeye, Arizona. Sonoran Logistics Park will be LogiPropco’s third development in the Phoenix area. Construction is expected to commence in the fourth quarter of 2026. When complete, Sonoran Logistics Park will total 1,226,832 square feet across two buildings featuring 36’–40’ clear heights with more than 15,000 amps of power available. The park’s location offers immediate access to Interstate 10, is within three miles of Loop 303, and is approximately 30 miles from Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.  Logistics Property Company’s Brad Cushard and Andrew Spiegel worked with Cushman & Wakefield’s Andy Markham, Michael Haenel, and Phil Haenel on the transaction. The Cushman & Wakefield team will also serve as the project’s leasing representatives. Markham added, “The west valley of metropolitan Phoenix is seeing record absorption and robust demand for bulk warehousing and manufacturing facilities.” Sonoran Logistics Park is expected to deliver in early 2028. The post LogiPropCo Adding 1.2M-SF Logistics Facility to Phoenix Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: LogiPropCo closes 76-acre site, Buckeye AZ (I-10 & Perryville); Sonoran Logistics Park, 1.23M SF.
Two buildings, 36-40' clear heights; construction Q4 2026; delivery early 2028; 15K+ amps power.
West Valley Phoenix seeing record logistics absorption; signals industrial job growth, secondary residential demand lift.
stories.summary: Logistics Property Company closed on a 76-acre site in Buckeye, Arizona (at I-10 and Perryville Road) for Sonoran Logistics Park, its third Phoenix-area development. The project will deliver 1.23 million square feet across two buildings with 36–40 foot clear heights and 15,000+ amps of power. Construction begins Q4 2026; delivery is early 2028. The site sits 30 miles from Sky Harbor International Airport and offers immediate I-10 access.
stories.impact: West Valley Phoenix logistics build-out signals robust industrial job creation and supply-chain facility expansion in the Buckeye/west valley corridor. Increased logistics employment and population density in a historically underdeveloped submarket creates secondary demand for workforce housing (apartments, workforce-focused product) in West Valley communities; window to site/acquire multifamily assets in Buckeye, Surprise, Goodyear submarkets ahead of 2028 delivery.

stories.title: Publix to Anchor Retail Component of Matthews Planned Development
stories.excerpt: Publix will anchor the 82-acre Cadia Matthews mixed-use development at Stallings and Idlewild roads. Pappas Properties has begun work on the retail phase of its master-planned development in Matthews, which will be anchored by the well-known grocery chain. The Charlotte Business Journal reports sitework is nearly complete, and construction is expected to begin later this fall.at the 120,000-square-foot commercial village at Cadia Village. The first retail buildings are scheduled to be delivered in June, and the quick-service restaurant will be delivered next fall. The development will include a bank and a 12,000-square-foot, stand-alone medical office building. Thrift Commercial Real Estate Services is handling retail leasing. Choate Construction is the general contractor for the retail village and Publix store. At full buildout, Cadia Village Matthews will have 570 total residential units with a mix of for-sale and rental product types. The post Publix to Anchor Retail Component of Matthews Planned Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Cadia Matthews, Matthews NC: 82-acre mixed-use; Publix anchors 120K SF retail village; 570 total units.
Sitework nearly complete; retail delivery June 2025, QSR fall 2025; mix of for-sale and rental residential.
Suburban Charlotte submarket gaining anchored retail; signals growth/desirability; rental units component de-risks multifamily demand.
stories.summary: Pappas Properties is developing Cadia Matthews, an 82-acre mixed-use project in Matthews, North Carolina, anchored by Publix grocery in a 120,000-square-foot retail village. Sitework is nearly complete; retail buildings deliver June 2025, with QSR (restaurant) and standalone 12,000-square-foot medical office in fall 2025. At full buildout, Cadia will include 570 total residential units (for-sale and rental mix).
stories.impact: Publix anchor and 570-unit mixed-use buildout signal strong demand and developer confidence in Matthews submarket, a key growth suburb southeast of Charlotte. The rental component (units count not specified) embedded in anchored retail signals multifamily absorption capacity; confirms southeast Charlotte corridor as active development zone. Anchored retail/mixed-use model de-risks rental units, validating submarket as target for additional standalone multifamily development.

stories.title: Fifth Wall’s Brendan Wallace On Spotting Real Estate’s Next Hot Tech Early
stories.excerpt: Stratford Wallace’s family had owned a lot on the Southeast corner of 41st Street and Eighth Avenue in Manhattan since 1886. Then, in the early aughts, the State of New York used eminent domain to wrestle the land from the Wallace family’s control. Wallace told Forbes in 2008 that, had he been given the chance to negotiate, he would have asked for $30 million. However, according to his son Brendan Wallace, the eminent domain declaration left him no choice but to accept the $12 million offered by the Empire State Development Corporation, the state’s economic development agency. Today, that lot, along with several adjacent others, is the site of the New York Times Building. The younger Wallace, 44, is the founder of Fifth Wall, which bills itself as “the largest investment firm focused on technology for the built environment.” Since its inception, the firm has received commitments of approximately $3.1 billion from roughly 115 limited partners, including CBRE, Hilton, Hines, Marriott, Public Storage, Related Companies and Starwood. Wallace recalls walking around the city as a child with his father, visiting his father’s properties and developing an early obsession with land in the process. (Stratford Wallace died in 2022 at age 85.) “Land is the input to the entire economy, and the one asset they’re not making more of,” said Wallace. “And, it’s anti-inflationary. If you look at land values, they have outpaced basically every other measure of nominal and real growth.” The Los Angeles-based Wallace, a sports enthusiast and history buff, was a newlywed of three weeks as of his late September conversation with Commercial Observer. With degrees in political science and economics from Princeton and an MBA from Stanford, he is also a veteran of Goldman Sachs and Blackstone who could have worked in any industry. bullets: Fifth Wall founder Brendan Wallace; $3.1B raised from 115 LPs (CBRE, Hilton, Hines, Marriott, Public Storage).
Focus: proptech and AI for built environment; firm invests in real estate technology innovation.
Proptech fundraising surge signals capital flow to real estate tech; operational efficiency gains lower development costs.
stories.summary: Brendan Wallace, founder of Fifth Wall (a $3.1 billion proptech venture fund with 115 limited partners including CBRE, Hilton, Hines, Marriott, and Public Storage), sits at the nexus of real estate technology and capital allocation. Fifth Wall focuses exclusively on technology for the built environment. Wallace's family history includes eminent domain loss of Manhattan land (early 2000s, $12 million settlement; site now occupied by NY Times Building).
stories.impact: Rising proptech capital and investor appetite signals accelerating integration of AI, data, and automation into real estate operations. Developers should expect cost-reduction opportunities in construction tech, leasing platforms, and building operations software. However, proptech capital flow is independent of multifamily supply/demand fundamentals; unlikely to materially shift underwriting or feasibility of new multifamily development in near term.

stories.title: Power Tech & AI 2026
stories.excerpt: Honestly, the introduction to Commercial Observer’s definitive annual list of the most consequential figures in real estate technology could be just two letters. Wanna guess which two? You nailed it: A and I. Every entrant on the list either noted, or is noted for, the eschatological technology. Generative artificial intelligence is now a force in data crunching, building operations, sustainability, leasing, sales, foot traffic tracking, location siting, repairs, maintenance and lending. It’s hard to find a cranny of commercial real estate that AI has not infiltrated. It’s the prime driver of the market’s most robust — and controversial — asset niche: data centers. And even longtime software as a service (SaaS) companies are leaning into AI, too, as MRI Software’s Patrick Ghilani, an honoree on the list, told us. Plus, the handful of early AI pioneers in the industry are doing funding and product victory laps. “We were building AI before ChatGPT existed, and we haven’t slowed down since,” said honoree Minna Song, whose EliseAI announced a fresh $350 million fundraise only last week. But it’s still early days, believe it or not. “Respectfully, it’s a little bit of a honeymoon period and it will change,” honoree Raj Singh of JLL Spark told us of commercial real estate’s passionate embrace of AI. How will AI’s relationship to CRE change? The pace of adoption will pick up, that’s for sure. “Institutional real estate has been slow and late to use generative, agentic AI in its workflows,” said Fifth Wall’s Brendan Wallace, another honoree. At the same time, the number of stand-alone AI firms servicing CRE will likely shrink amid competition and consolidation. Ironically, AI itself might foster this shrinkage through new efficiencies. “I don’t believe you’re going to see hundreds of successful AI companies in commercial real estate,” said honoree Nick Romito of VTS. bullets: AI is infiltrating all real estate niches: data centers, leasing, valuations, operations, maintenance, lending.
Early AI pioneers (EliseAI, JLL Spark) completing funding rounds; generative AI becoming standard tool.
AI-driven data centers are largest/most controversial asset class; proptech SaaS (MRI Software) integrating AI.
stories.summary: Generative AI has become a dominant force across commercial real estate—from data crunching and building operations to leasing, valuation, foot traffic tracking, repairs, and lending. Early proptech pioneers like EliseAI are announcing major funding ($350 million raises), while established SaaS platforms (MRI Software) are embedding AI capabilities. Data centers—driven by AI infrastructure demand—have become the most robust and controversial real estate niche.
stories.impact: AI-driven data center demand is creating a new, massive real estate category with outsized capital allocation and land/site acquisition urgency in major metros (Northern Virginia, Phoenix, Dallas, etc.). Developers should monitor AI hub formation and data center pipeline development in target markets; density of data centers and AI infrastructure can catalyze secondary office/multifamily demand (worker proximity, tech worker recruitment). However, article provides no specific market or deal signal; is trend commentary only.
